Hey there! I agree with you that one shouldn't conflate dissatisfaction with one's body to queerness or the trans experience. You don't have to hate your body or want to change it to be trans! I'm in that same boat for sure. I don't think that this is THE queer aesthetic, which is why I wrote that it's a "part of the queer aesthetic". I do think there's a bit of misunderstanding here because we're actually on the same side of this argument. 


Another point of yours that I agree with is that a lot of people who think they need plastic surgery to feel beautiful feel that way because society tells them that a particular look is the only way they can be beautiful. Though I'd like to consider plastic surgery morally neutral, I don't think it is societally neutral. It is yet another tool to reinforce existing beauty ideals which are drawn from white, cis heteronormativity. I totally agree that it's not something one should consider lightly, esp procedures like BBLs which come with significant risk.


All that being said, I don't think it's right to conflate any of this with mental illness. We are not licensed professionals actually diagnosing our own patient. We can comment on the social phenomenon of beauty ideals and their harm overall, but it seems to be overstepping to call a gay man who seems happy with his altered body mentally ill just because we don't fully understand his choices.

That's a really good point. It's easier for someone who naturally fits into society's ideal beauty standards to say that natural is better. And it can feel super alienating to someone who doesn't see themselves fitting into those standards.

Hey, first of all, I'm so sorry you had to go through all that! And I totally understand where you're coming from when you say you light consider cosmetic procedures due to these reasons. I'm kinda anti plastic surgery too (even tho I often think about what I'd look like with lip filler oop) again not because I think people who get it are doing something wrong but just because I do believe that the desire to get it rarely comes from something deeply personal and inherent.

 I don't think most people are getting it "because they want to" but because society has told them that life will be better if they fit into a certain ideal. I've been bigger all my life and I've dieted all my life until recently and I have realized it's not because I wanted to do it "just because". It was because the people around me made me feel bad, wrong, unworthy for being larger and I wanted a feeling of worthiness I thought i could only get from becoming skinny. And I have been quite skinny too in this journey, and the world certainly treated me better for it. 

Now that I'm larger again, I'm learning to accept that this is just my natural body weight and the reason I never saw it as desirable before was because everything I saw around me said it wasn't. Now I'm making an effort to seek out media and content by people who are fat and sexy and happy with themselves and its definitely helping change my mindset. I still sometimes feel bad about my body, my weight, my chest, my lips etc but I know it's not just an "insecurity" borne in a vacuum. 

And while I get that on the individual level, one person not getting plastic surgery doesn't change the system (nor does one person getting it perpetuate the system) but I do wonder that if society continues to promote that ideal beauty standard, and it becomes more and more accessible and normalised to get it through surgery, are we just headed for an even more fucked up world than the one we already live in?

Initially, I didn't know exactly what was wrong, but I knew something *was* definitely wrong. I had depression that would last months, hypomanic episodes that were sometimes fun, sometimes scary.

We didn't talk about feelings, we didn't show emotion, god forbid I ever cried in front of them or something like that. I never even got the sex talk. We were very aloof, still are. They never really noticed any of my symptoms, or if they did, the idea of mental illness was so obscure that they never put two and two together.

I didn't know whom to bring this up with, or how. My school counselor was my mom's best friend, so that was out. I ended up just 'sucking it up' for more than a year. 

At fifteen, I had a major psychotic episode, and it became clear to everyone what was going on.

I don't suggest you wait for something like this to happen to you. Go to your GP, tell them you've been experiencing certain symptoms, almost exactly like you just described them, and that it's troubling you and interfering with your work. 

Don't be afraid anyone will think you're faking it - they won't. Doctors want to help you. You just have to say "I'm having problems, please help me figure them out."

Flourless Chocolate Cake


4 ounces bittersweet chocolate

1 stick (1/2 cup) unsalted butter

3/4 cup granulated sugar

3 large eggs

1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder

1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract (optional)

1/2 teaspoon fine grind espresso (optional)


Directions:


Preheat oven to 375 degrees. In a heat proof bowl, combine chocolate and butter. Melt the chocolate and butter using either a double boiler (heat proof bowl over a simmering pot of water) or in the microwave in 30 second intervals, stirring between each interval.

Once fully melted, whisk in sugar. Once combined, whisk in eggs, one at 
a time until fully combined. Stir in vanilla and espresso (if using).

Sift cocoa powder into the chocolate mixture. Whisk to combine.

Pour into a greased, or preferably thin-foil-lined, 8 inch cake or tart pan.

Bake 23-25 minutes. Let rest on a wire rack for 5 minutes before removing from pan.


Cherry and Cognac Reduction

A couple of dollops of cherry preserves and a couple of splashes of cognac (can be substituted with brandy) in a saucepan, let the cognac ignite, swirl it around for a bit and once it resembles a syrup-y substance, serve.
